pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 2, later: Growing: a tortoise. Also a headache.*

I did not scream. I made a sound that was mostly air and slightly less dignity, and my feet left the ground.

In the grass sat a tortoise. It was the size of a hat, with a shell that looked like a mossy cobblestone and eyes the color of wet raisins. It blinked. The blink took longer than I cared to count.

"Mm," it said. The voice was deep and dry, like a leaf rustling in a windless room. "My name is... Gherkin."

I stared. He stared back. I counted. It took eleven seconds for him to finish the word.

"I am... three... hundred... years... old," he continued. His head moved forward, an inch at a time. "More... or... less."

Nine seconds. I was still holding the seed packet. My fingers were trembling.

"And you have... picked up... the wrong... seed."

Forty seconds. I looked at the packet in my hand. *Patience Pea*. I looked at Gherkin. He was already looking at the grass again, waiting for me to realize the conversation had ended.
pages.image: A girl in a denim jacket stands frozen on tiptoes above a large mossy tortoise in tall grass, holding a seed packet with wide eyes, while the tortoise looks up slowly with ancient calm.

pages.text:
Gherkin moved. Or rather, he suggested movement. His front left leg extended, an inch, then another, then a pause that lasted long enough for me to check my watch.

"You are the sort," he said, "who digs up... a seed... to see... if it is... working."

I felt heat rise in my neck. "I did that," I said. "Twice."

"Twice," he repeated. The word dragged out like taffy. "That is... quite... a lot... for... one... week."

He turned his head. It was a full rotation, but it felt like it took an hour. I wanted to say that I was actually very careful. I wanted to say that I had read the book. I wanted to say that I was not the kind of person who ruins things because they are bored. But he was looking at me with those wet raisin eyes, and I knew he knew I was lying. Not because I lied, but because I had done it. Twice.

"The bean," I said, trying to sound casual, "is fine now."

"Mm," said Gherkin. "We shall... see."
pages.image: A close-up of the mossy tortoise’s head turned sideways, its eye focused on the girl, with tall blades of grass framing the scene, conveying a sense of slow, unblinking judgment.

pages.text:
I dropped onto the grass, my knees still trembling from the earlier jump. A three-hundred-year-old tortoise sat three feet away, and I had absolutely no idea what to do with my hands.

"This garden," Gherkin said, "has been... waiting... a long... time... for... somebody... to come... through... the fence."

"Did you mean a gardener?" I asked.

"Not a gardener," he replied. "Anybody... would do."

"Really?"

"Really," he confirmed. "It has... only one... requirement."

My heart did a little flip. "Patience?"

"Patience," he said.

I looked down at my hands, then at the seed packet in my lap. The bean in its yogurt cup came to mind, along with the list taped to our fridge. *Know where the bus goes. Have one friend.* I wanted those things by Friday, the bean to sprout by tomorrow, and to be good at this by now.

"That is... possibly," I said, "a problem."

Gherkin blinked. It took four seconds.

"Mm," he said. "Possibly."
pages.image: The girl sits cross-legged in the grass, looking down at her hands, while the tortoise watches from a short distance, the background a blur of green leaves and soft afternoon light.

pages.text:
I picked up the brass trowel. It felt different now, heavier, or maybe I was just heavier.

"The tin," I said. "The rules. Are they real?"

Gherkin lifted his head. "The rules... are real."

"What happens if I break them?"

The tortoise let out a sound that might have been a sigh. "The garden... does not punish... anybody."

"Then what does it do?"

"It exaggerates," he said.

I frowned. "Exaggerates?"

"A seed... planted in a hurry... grows in a hurry," he said. "And wrong."

"A true word... makes it grow right."

I looked at the *Patience Pea* packet, then at the dirt. The sun was warm on the back of my neck, and the trowel sat heavy in my hand. I could feel the impulse to just dig, to plant, to see, to have, to be done.

"It’s not that simple," I said.

"Mm," said Gherkin. "No. It is... much... simpler."
pages.image: The girl holds the brass trowel in one hand and the seed packet in the other, looking down at a patch of dark soil, with the tortoise visible in the soft-focus background.

pages.text:
I set the seed packet down, then picked it up again, my thumb rubbing the printed image of the green pea.

"Okay," I said. "I want to plant one. Right now."

Gherkin remained perfectly still. "You may... plant one... seed... a day... and no more."

"I’m not planning to plant forty-one," I clarified. "I am going to plant exactly one."

I chose the *Patience Pea*. It seemed like the right choice, which was ironic given my current state. I dug a small hole with the brass trowel, the soil loose and smelling strongly of recent rain. Placing the seed in the center, I patted the earth down with my thumb.

I did not say a true thing. I had completely forgotten the second rule.

Standing up, I brushed the dirt from my knees and stared at the spot I had just covered. It looked like ordinary dirt, nothing more, holding nothing but a small brown object that expected me to remember what I had just broken.

Gherkin watched me. His eyelids lowered slowly, a process that took six full seconds to complete.

"Mm," he said. "We shall... see."
pages.image: The girl stands up, brushing dirt from her denim jacket, looking back at a small, neat hole in the ground, with the tortoise watching intently from the side.
